newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Bulgaria, Serbia unrest reflects E. Europe divide.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria, Serbia unrest reflects E. Europe divide.

text.p: Bulgarian and Serbian-style popular unrest seems a distant prospect in other states of Central Europe, reflecting a new divide in economic and political developments in the region since the fall of communism.
On the surface, the displays of people power in Belgrade and Sofia are reminiscent of the mass popular revolutions which overturned communist governments at the end of 1989.
But differing rates of economic and political development have created new divisions among the former socialist bloc.
Pressure is growing on Bulgaria's ex-communist rulers to hold an early general election as trade unions began warning strikes after more than a week of protests inspired by economic crisis.

In neighbouring Serbia, the opposition urged hundreds of thousands of people to turn out on Monday for an Orthodox calendar New Year's Eve demonstration they hope will be the biggest yet against President Slobodan Milosevic.
Students and the Zajedno (Together) opposition have held daily protests for almost two months to force the government to reinstate the results of municipal elections.
"The underlying problem is the economy because it is in a very bad state in both countries," said Jiri Pehe, research director of the Open Media Research Institute in Prague.
"Also, in both those countries there are the strongest vestiges of communism, of the former regime," he added.

The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary, with vibrant economies, have developed strong democratic institutions and are seen as the most likely to be accepted as members of the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
Hungary's Socialist Prime Minister Gyula Horn said unrest in Serbia and Bulgaria was a result of the two socialist governments delaying democratic reforms.

"(The problems of both countries') democratic transformation and the normal operation of the system have not been solved, while in Bulgaria (social and economic) reforms have not yet even begun," he told a news conference on Monday.

Poland's "shock therapy" of financial austerity, trade liberalisation and privatisation, curbed hyperinflation, liquidated communist-era queues and filled shops with goods. The economy is now expanding by 5 to 6 percent annually.

"If we had postponed major reforms, as they did in Bulgaria, we would have been in a similar situation, we would have had riots, queues, strikes and bitterness," said Piotr Nowina-Konopka, an analyst and opposition parliamentarian.

The Czech Republic has been lauded by foreign investors for its fiscal prudence. Monetarist Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's government, elected in 1992, is the longest surviving right-wing government in post-communist Europe.
But reform has lagged in the Balkans.
Communists have ruled in Serbia without interruption since 1945, surviving the 1989 revolutions. The economy has been devastated by international sanctions.

The election to the Bulgarian presidency last November of opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov sparkled a wave of opposition to the ex-Communist Bulgarian Socialist Party which has headed seven of the eight governments since 1989.
Bulgaria's month-on-month inflation soared to 26.9 percent in December from just over nine percent in November after a series of price increases on basic food and fuel items.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank suspended funding over the Socialist government's failure to reduce budget-draining subsidies and boost revenue through sell-offs.

Pehe said Bulgarian protesters took heart from elections in neighbouring Romania last November when Romanians, disgruntled over soaring prices and growing poverty, pushed ex-president Ion Iliescu's leftists out of office.
The Fund also froze credits for Romania last year over the policies of the former administration. The ruling centrist coalition will resume loan talks later this month.

But local economists say a repeat of the political and labour unrest which shook Romania in the early post-communist years is unlikely, with Romanians bracing themselves for the tough reforms needed to put the economy on track.
